cases.abstract: VoxPoser translates language-specified manipulation subtasks into robot trajectories by using pretrained language models to construct spatial objectives rather than directly parameterizing action primitives. Generated programs query visual perception and compose three-dimensional voxel maps of task affordances and constraints; motion planning uses these maps to guide end-effector or object motion, with repeated replanning from updated observations. This representation supports zero-shot trajectory synthesis without additional training, while allowing synthesized trajectories to guide subsequent dynamics learning. Across five tabletop robot tasks, success averages 88% without disturbances and 70% with disturbances, compared with 24% and 0% for a language-model-plus-primitives baseline. In a 13-task simulation suite, category-level results favor VoxPoser over both that baseline and learned costmaps, including unseen instructions and attributes, although individual tasks do not uniformly improve. Contact-intensive simulated door, window, and fridge tasks expose poor zero-shot success; using synthesized trajectories as exploration priors enables dynamics learning with under three minutes of online interaction, whereas exploration without priors exceeds a twelve-hour limit. Thus, spatial composition extends language-driven manipulation beyond primitive sequencing, but performance remains limited by perception and environment dynamics, and the implementation plans end-effector rather than whole-arm trajectories.
cases.notes: Central contribution: spatially composing language-derived objectives for trajectory planning, not high-level task decomposition. Sections 3.2-3.4 and Tables 1-3 support zero-shot synthesis, disturbance handling, generalization, and exploration-guided dynamics learning as a co-contribution. Table 4 prevents a per-task superiority claim. Contact results are simulated and require learning; Table 3 dispersion is not defined. Perception failures and end-effector-only planning are substantive boundaries. Zero-shot uses pretrained models and manually supplied prompt examples.

cases.abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) seeks better generalization by minimizing worst-case training loss within a parameter neighborhood, with weight regularization, instead of loss at a single point. A PAC-Bayesian bound motivates this objective, conditional on Gaussian perturbations not reducing population loss and a parameter-norm assumption. SAM approximates neighborhood maximization with a gradient-directed weight perturbation and then updates using the gradient at the perturbed weights, discarding second-order terms. Each update requires two backpropagations. In CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 experiments, SAM improves every tested configuration against baselines allowed up to twice as many epochs; an AutoAugment WideResNet reduces CIFAR-10 error from 2.2% to 1.6%. ImageNet training and pretrained EfficientNet finetuning also improve, with ImageNet-plus-JFT-pretrained EfficientNet-L2 reaching 0.30% CIFAR-10 error. Under random label corruption, SAM improves clean-test accuracy but trails MentorMix; bootstrapping narrows this gap without removing it at the highest noise rate. Hessian analyses find lower curvature, and smaller subsets improve both SAM training and the predictive value of m-sharpness in the studied settings. Benefits are not universal: one augmented SVHN configuration worsens. The results support an implementable neighborhood-loss objective, without making the conditional bound a guarantee for the minibatch approximation.
cases.notes: Central contribution: replacing pointwise empirical-risk minimization with a tractable neighborhood-loss objective; theory motivates rather than certifies the implementation. Theorem 2 conditions include nondecreasing expected population loss under Gaussian perturbations and parameter norm at least one. Table 1 comparisons allow longer non-SAM training, unlike a blanket matched-epoch claim. Tables 3-5 preserve finetuning, noisy-label benefits, and the SVHN reversal. Section 4 supplies the m-sharpness co-contribution and geometric diagnostics. No universal improvement or unconditional practical generalization guarantee is asserted.
